items.title: Kyla Scanlon asks Claudia Sahm why it is so hard to find a job right now
items.why: Sahm invented the recession indicator that bears her name, so she is a better person than most to ask whether a tough job hunt is you or the economy. Expect a calm walk through the data rather than a forecast with a thesis to sell.
items.summary: In the fourth episode of Kyla Scanlon's interview show Best of Luck, economist Claudia Sahm talks about why the job market feels so tight. They discuss what the indicators say and where that leaves people looking for work.

items.title: OOS: an open custom Linux firmware for newer Rigol scopes
items.why: Owning the oscilloscope and also owning the software running on it is a very late-90s sort of ambition. One hacker is building an open replacement for the stock firmware on Rigol's DHO series, which is the kind of project that turns a gadget into a platform.
items.summary: A developer known as dekajoule is writing OOS, an Open Operating System for Rigol's DHO line of oscilloscopes released in 2022. It is a custom Linux-based firmware meant as an open alternative to the factory software.

items.title: Why rich Renaissance Europeans collected unicorn horns
items.why: Cabinets of curiosities were part museum, part status symbol and part early lab notebook, and the 'unicorn horns' in them were mostly narwhal tusks. Evan Puschak's video uses them to look at a moment when collectors were starting to trust their own eyes over ancient authorities.
items.summary: A short video essay on wunderkammers, the cabinets of curios and natural oddities that wealthy Europeans assembled during the Renaissance. It traces how the practice grew alongside the scientific revolution and what the objects said about how people were rethinking knowledge.

items.title: The scimitar-horned oryx is back in Chad, 700 strong
items.why: A small dose of unambiguous good news: an antelope declared extinct in the wild in 2000 now has the largest wild herd anywhere, and its status has been upgraded. Twenty-five animals in 2016 to seven hundred now is the kind of curve worth staring at.
items.summary: The scimitar-horned oryx vanished from Chad by the late 1980s, but a reintroduction programme in the Ouadi Rimé–Ouadi Achim reserve has grown the population from 25 to about 700. The species' global status has improved from extinct in the wild to endangered.

items.title: How Linux's core operations got slower over seven years, via The Morning Paper
items.why: A SOSP'19 paper that benchmarked the kernel's bread-and-butter syscalls across years of releases and found many had regressed or wobbled. Anyone who has bisected a performance drop to a well-meaning security mitigation or a default flipped in a config will nod along; Colyer's honest note that the lessons are hard to act on is the most useful part.
items.summary: Adrian Colyer's write-up of Ren et al.'s study of how the performance of Linux's core operations evolved across seven years of kernels. Many operations got slower or fluctuated, mostly because of new features, security hardening and changed defaults rather than outright bugs.

items.title: An astronaut stepping across a roundabout in Valdemoro, Spain
items.why: Spanish roundabouts are a whole genre of public sculpture, and this one sends a four-metre stainless-steel astronaut striding across a lunar surface in the middle of suburban traffic. Whether he is planting a flag or looking for a gap in the cars is left to the viewer.
items.summary: Francisco Leiro's sculpture El Astronauta has stood on a roundabout in Valdemoro, south of Madrid, since 2001. The tall steel figure mid-stride on a moonscape has become the town's best-known modern landmark.

items.title: China outlines a plan to land on Callisto
items.why: Everyone wants Europa, the moon with the ocean and the headlines. Callisto is the heavily cratered, geologically sleepy sibling, which is exactly why it's a good archive of the Jovian system's history. A two-instrument lander sounds modest until you remember how far away it is.
items.summary: China has sketched plans to put a small lander on Callisto, the outermost of Jupiter's four big moons. It would be only the second landing on any body beyond Mars, carrying two proposed instruments.

items.title: Punch Brothers and Jeff Tweedy confirm a joint tour, billed as PB&J
items.why: Chris Thile and company have form when it comes to collaborations, and Tweedy's loose, rumpled songwriting against that string-band precision should make for an interesting sandwich. The name is a groaner; the bill is not.
items.summary: Punch Brothers and Wilco's Jeff Tweedy have confirmed they will tour together as a shared bill under the name PB&J. It pairs the string-band quintet with one of Americana's more restless songwriters for a run of shared shows.

items.title: Hintighernia edingerae, a new tapejarid pterosaur named for Tilly Edinger
items.why: Not a dinosaur, strictly, but the palaeontology desk does not stand on ceremony. The species name is the quiet joy here: Tilly Edinger fled Nazi Germany and more or less invented the study of fossil brains, and a crested flier is a fitting tribute.
items.summary: Palaeontologists have described a new species of tapejarid, the family of pterosaurs known for their flamboyant head crests. Its name honours Tilly Edinger, the German-American palaeontologist who founded palaeoneurology after escaping Nazi persecution.

items.title: Paludohadros proudlovii: a new iguanodontian from a Surrey brickworks quarry
items.why: Twenty-five years in a museum drawer is a respectable gestation period for a dinosaur, and this one came out of the clay pits that feed a brick factory. Note the namesake: not a professor but a local man from Surrey, which is a nicer kind of immortality than most of us get.
items.summary: Bones dug from a Surrey clay quarry in 2001, around 132 million years old, have been described as a new iguanodontian dinosaur, Paludohadros proudlovii. The roughly five-metre animal sat in the Natural History Museum's collections for decades before a fresh look showed it was something new.

items.title: A firefly not seen since 1983 is flashing in Delaware again
items.why: An entomologist standing in a meadow with a camera, spotting an amber flash pattern that didn't match anything he knew, and being right. The similar firefly had gone undocumented for over forty years before turning up again this year, which is the kind of conservation story that leaves you calmer rather than angrier. Bonus nerd point: the species was identified from its flash rhythm alone.
items.summary: Mongabay reports that Pyractomena similis, a firefly species last documented in 1983, has been found again in Delaware. Entomologist Christopher Heckscher picked it out by its distinctive amber flash and long rhythmic pattern, and further sightings followed in 2026.

items.title: A 1966 poem made only of the kanji for river and sandbank
items.why: Futility Closet in its natural habitat: one small, perfect object and almost no commentary. Seiichi Niikuni's poem tiles two characters into triangles so the page becomes a picture of the thing it names, a river running along a bank. Concrete poetry rarely gets this tidy, and it helps that the two characters already look a bit like what they mean.
items.summary: A short note on Seiichi Niikuni's 1966 visual poem River/Sandbank, which consists entirely of the Japanese characters for river and sandbank. Each is repeated to fill a right triangle, and together they form a square that depicts its own subject.

items.title: Harold A. Taylor's early colour photographs of California flowers
items.why: Autochromes are the early colour process that used dyed potato-starch grains on glass, and they give everything a soft, pointillist glow that no modern sensor bothers to imitate. A collection of wildflowers by a photographer who championed California's natural beauty is about as calm as an archive pick gets. Good for a slow scroll.
items.summary: The Public Domain Review gathers early twentieth century autochrome photographs of flowers by Harold A. Taylor, a photographer who promoted California's landscapes. The images are early colour plates of the state's flora, now in the public domain.

items.title: Apple's Neuromancer series will give the Tessier-Ashpools more room than the book did
items.why: Adapting Gibson is a bit like adapting a fever dream with excellent prose rhythm, so it's reassuring that the showrunners are talking about what to add rather than what to sand down. The Tessier-Ashpool clan, all cold money and orbital decadence, were always the part of the novel with the most unexplored corridors. Whether that's a good idea is a fine argument to have over a cup of something.
items.summary: Reactor reports that the Neuromancer TV adaptation for Apple TV will expand the Tessier-Ashpool storyline beyond what appears in William Gibson's novel. The showrunners say they intend to stay true to the book's spirit while departing from it where the series format allows.

items.title: Designing data structures for far memory, via The Morning Paper
items.why: From the archive: Adrian Colyer on Aguilera and colleagues' HotOS 2019 paper about memory that sits on the network and is read without bothering the remote CPU. The argument is that one-sided access only pays off if a lookup finishes in a single far access most of the time, which quietly rules out most textbook structures. The fun part is how far down the stack that requirement reaches, all the way to what the…
items.summary: A summary of a HotOS 2019 paper on far memory, meaning network-attached memory accessed without a remote processor in the loop. It weighs the benefits, such as capacity, independent scaling and separate fault domains, against the cost of multiple round trips, and argues for new data structures that usually need just one far access per operation, with hardware support to match.

items.title: Two firmware typos behind the Wii U's blurry Wii mode, found and fixed
items.why: A proper hobbyist deep dive: Wii games on a Wii U have looked worse than on an actual Wii since 2013, with cropped output and colour bleed, and nobody official ever fixed it. The author follows the trail into the little 68HC11-compatible microcontroller that emulates the old Wii video interface, and finds two simple typos in its firmware. The aside that modern AMD GPUs share bits of this display hardware is the…
items.summary: A technical write-up on why the Wii U's backwards-compatible Wii mode shows cropped, colour-smeared video. It explains how a small dedicated microcontroller translates the old Wii display settings onto the console's Radeon-derived graphics hardware, and how two mistakes in that firmware cause the problems, along with a fix.

items.title: Birding lodges of the world: Araucana Lodge in Colombia's cloud forest
items.why: Colombia has more bird species than anywhere else, which makes a lodge Q&A less a travel brochure and more a list of reasons to book a flight. The headline bird here is the Multicolored Tanager, a Colombian endemic that looks like someone ran out of restraint with the paint box. Useful reading for a solo birder who likes to know where the good cloud forest trails start.
items.summary: 10,000 Birds continues its lodge series with a short interview about Araucana Lodge in Colombia, a base for exploring the nearby San Antonio cloud forest and the KM18 area. The owners name the endemic Multicolored Tanager as the star attraction and describe what visiting birders can expect.

items.title: Twenty years of the Dark Energy Survey, and a hint that the books don't balance
items.why: Quanta does the long view on dark energy, told partly through Joshua Frieman, who remembers when it was a niche idea that could barely fill a workshop in 1997. A survey that took two decades to plan, run and analyse now suggests the standard cosmological model may be missing something. Cosmic bookkeeping at its finest, with appropriately cautious accountants.
items.summary: A feature on the two-decade Dark Energy Survey and what its results suggest about the makeup of the universe. It traces how dark energy went from a fringe proposal in the 1990s to the dominant ingredient in cosmology, and why the latest results hint that the accepted picture may need revising.

items.title: A white dwarf and an ordinary star that pulse in radio every few minutes
items.why: Long-period radio transients are one of the better recent puzzles: things that blip in radio on timescales of minutes, far too slow for a normal pulsar. This one breaks the pattern by pairing its white dwarf with a main-sequence star instead of the usual red dwarf. The bonus is the supernova angle, since binaries like this could be a common route to Type Ia explosions.
items.summary: Astronomers have found a long-period radio transient about 5,000 light years away made of a white dwarf and a main-sequence companion, unlike the white dwarf and red dwarf pairs seen before. The cause of its radio pulses is still uncertain, but the system narrows the options and hints that such pairs may often end as Type Ia supernovae.

items.title: A big orca relative was hunting the North Sea more than two million years ago
items.why: Not a dinosaur, but the palaeontology slot takes what the seabed gives it, and this one has teeth. Fossil killer whales are scarce enough that every new taxon helps pin down when the modern orca's lineage got big and bold. Worth noticing is the timing: the earliest Pleistocene, just as the ice ages were getting into their stride and the North Sea was a very different body of water.
items.summary: Researchers describe a large killer whale relative that lived in the North Sea at the very start of the Pleistocene, over two million years ago. The find adds an early, sizeable member to the orca family tree and suggests big predatory dolphins were already patrolling northern European waters back then.

items.title: Punch Brothers bring their string-band chamber music to Carmel, Indiana
items.why: Favourite-band rule, and the fall tour keeps working its way across the Midwest. The local paper is previewing a stop at the Palladium, a concert hall that was built with acoustic music in mind, which is about the right room for a band that treats a mandolin quintet like a small orchestra. File it with the other dates ahead of February's PB&J run with Jeff Tweedy.
items.summary: Current, a local paper in Carmel, Indiana, previews the Punch Brothers' visit to the Palladium at the Center for the Performing Arts, booked for November 20. The piece pitches the band's mix of bluegrass instrumentation and inventive, classically minded arrangements to a local audience.

items.title: Falling and rising seas may explain why the Ediacaran fossils survived so well
items.why: Not a dinosaur, but the fossils from the very start of complex animal life, which is the story every dinosaur story is a sequel to. The interesting bit is that the preservation itself is the subject: the Ediacara beds owe their extraordinary detail to big swings in sea level that carved and then refilled seafloor canyons. Taphonomy, the science of how things get lucky enough to become fossils, rarely gets a headline.
items.summary: A study led by Adelaide University looked at rocks in South Australia that hold some of the oldest known complex animals. It argues that sea levels dropped and then rose sharply, cutting submarine canyons whose fill helped preserve the soft-bodied Ediacaran organisms in unusual detail.

items.title: A type Ia supernova goes off just 50 million light-years away
items.why: Fifty million light-years counts as next door for a type Ia, and nearby ones are rare enough that astronomers drop what they are doing. These exploding white dwarfs are the standard candles behind the measurement of cosmic expansion, so getting a close, early look at one helps calibrate the yardstick everyone else uses. The fun part is that the observing campaign runs for years as the light fades.
items.summary: Astronomers have spotted a new type Ia supernova, the thermonuclear explosion of a white dwarf, in a spiral galaxy roughly 50 million light-years away. Because it is so close, follow-up observations started quickly and will track how its light changes over the coming days, months and years.

items.title: Three sizes of black: sorting the corvids of Xinjiang
items.why: A birder in Xinjiang sorts the local corvids the way a clothing shop sorts T-shirts, which is a better field guide than it sounds. Jackdaw for small, a pair of half-kilo crows for medium, and you can guess what fills out the large. Light, funny and quietly useful for anyone who has ever squinted at a black bird and given up.
items.summary: A post on 10,000 Birds walks through the black corvids seen on a trip to Xinjiang in far western China, grouped by size. The jackdaw is the small one, two crow species share the middle ground at around half a kilogram each, and the larger birds round out the set, with photographs from the trip.

items.title: A LEGO marigold bridge from Coco for one last Día de los Muertos
items.why: The petal bridge between the living and the dead is one of the loveliest images in Coco, and it is all gradient, which is not something LEGO normally does well. Jean-Philippe Leroux makes it work with the newer plant pieces and colours, blending them so smoothly the bricks almost disappear. Worth a close look at how the orange shades are layered.
items.summary: Builder Jean-Philippe Leroux has recreated the glowing marigold-petal bridge from Pixar's Coco, the path that links the lands of the living and the dead. The Brothers Brick highlights how recent plant elements and colours let him build a near-seamless orange gradient across the span.

items.title: A plaque in Mantua for Agnese Visconti, beheaded in 1391
items.why: Mantua's Ducal Palace is the sort of place where people stand under famous frescoes, so it is fitting that one of the more striking stops is a plain stone plaque few tourists notice. It marks a grim chapter of Renaissance dynastic politics, a fourteen-year-old bride married into one great house and executed by it. Quiet square, loud history.
items.summary: Atlas Obscura describes a simple memorial plaque on the wall of a tree-lined square within the grounds of the Ducal Palace in Mantua. It commemorates Agnese Visconti, daughter of the lord of Milan, who was married young to Francesco I Gonzaga and beheaded there in 1391 after he accused her of adultery.

items.title: Svofski builds a cassette deck mechanism from scratch
items.why: With almost nobody still making tape transports, someone was bound to try building one from first principles. This design skips the capstan entirely: each spool gets its own brushless motor, and an optical mouse sensor reads the tape speed to close the loop. It is the kind of gloriously unnecessary engineering the late-90s web was full of.
items.summary: Hackaday covers a homebrew cassette mechanism by the maker Svofski, built on a chassis made of circuit boards. Instead of the usual capstan and pinch roller, two brushless motors drive the reels directly and an optical mouse sensor measures tape movement to regulate speed.

items.title: How 40 big C projects actually manage memory
items.why: Anyone who has worked on a kernel knows malloc and free are where C memory management starts, not where it ends, and this survey puts numbers on it. Arenas and regions turn up far more often than the textbooks suggest, with refcounting and outright garbage collection hiding in plenty of household-name codebases. A good one to argue about over teh tarik.
items.summary: A survey of 40 well-known C codebases, including Linux, PostgreSQL, Git, QEMU and Lua, classifies how each one allocates memory. Only eight rely solely on malloc and free; fifteen use regions somewhere, seven allocate mainly with regions, five mainly with garbage collection and three mainly with reference counting.

items.title: Tolkien on fairy-stories, and why there is no such thing as writing for children
items.why: On Fairy-Stories is the closest Tolkien came to a manifesto, and it holds up remarkably well: fantasy as a sub-creation with its own rules, and the idea that children's literature is a shelf adults invented. Maria Popova pairs it with Sendak's matching opinion, which makes for a pleasing argument across generations. Read it, then go and reread the Hobbit without guilt.
items.summary: The Marginalian revisits J.R.R. Tolkien's essay on fairy-stories, drawing out his views on language, the psychology of fantasy and why the label of children's literature is arbitrary. The piece sets his thinking beside Maurice Sendak's remark that he never wrote for children, only wrote.

items.title: Porcelain cups the colour of the sky after rain
items.why: A short, unhurried film of potters making pale blue-green porcelain cups by traditional Chinese methods. The colour it chases has a legend attached, an emperor asking for ware the shade of the sky where rain clouds part, and the glaze gets remarkably close. Good for exactly the kind of idle minute this feed is for.
items.summary: Kottke shares a video showing porcelain cups being made by hand using traditional Chinese techniques, from shaping to glazing and firing. The aim is a soft blue glaze described as the colour of the sky after rain, where the clouds break apart.

items.title: Megapodius rokusi: a giant megapode turns up in the Flores cave of the hobbits
items.why: Liang Bua is the cave best known for Homo floresiensis, so it is pleasing that the island's oddities extend to the bird list. Megapodes are the birds that outsource egg-warming to sun, volcanic soil or rotting leaves, which makes a supersized one an appealing thing to picture scratching around Flores. Note the lead author's point that this is the first fossil megapode from anywhere in Indonesia, a country…
items.summary: Archaeologists working in Liang Bua on Flores have described a new species of extinct giant megapode that lived around 150,000 years ago. Megapodes are ground-nesting, chicken-like birds that warm their eggs with environmental heat instead of sitting on them; this is the first fossil one found in Indonesia.

items.title: Camera traps in Sarawak's mangroves catch the flat-headed cat at home in the palms
items.why: A neighbour of sorts: the flat-headed cat is one of Southeast Asia's least-studied mammals, and this survey ran just across the water in Sarawak. Three years of camera traps produced only 59 sightings, which tells you something about how good it is at not being seen. The flattened skull and forward-facing eyes are a fishing cat's toolkit, and the palm preference is the kind of detail that matters when someone draws…
items.summary: A camera-trap survey in the proposed Lundu Mangrove Protected Forest in southwestern Sarawak, run from 2021 to 2024, recorded the endangered flat-headed cat 59 times. The study sheds light on where and when this small, semi-aquatic fish-eating cat is active, including a preference for elevated palm habitat.

items.title: Hera gets its look at Didymos, the asteroid DART's target orbits
items.why: DART did the punching in 2022; Hera is the insurance assessor sent round afterwards to measure the dent properly. The first thing it has done is show us a cratered face of the parent asteroid Didymos, which matters because the deflection only makes sense once you know what kind of rubble you were pushing against. Planetary defence as careful bookkeeping rather than Hollywood.
items.summary: The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has returned views of a heavily cratered, previously unseen side of the asteroid Didymos as it closes in to study the binary system NASA's DART probe struck in 2022. Its measurements of the aftermath should help turn asteroid deflection from a one-off experiment into a usable technique.

items.title: The Long Earth as a map of how we live online, from Pratchett and Baxter
items.why: The Long Earth was always the odd one in the Pratchett shelf: co-written, earnest, and less fêted than the Discworld books. This essay argues that its endless parallel Earths, there for anyone to step into and settle, look a lot like the internet's frontier phase and the way people scatter into their own little worlds. A good excuse to dig the 2012 novel back out.
items.summary: A Reactor essay revisits Terry Pratchett and Stephen Baxter's 2012 novel The Long Earth, in which people can step into an endless chain of parallel Earths. The writer reads the book as an unexpectedly prescient picture of online life, with its frontier spirit and the urge to stake out spaces of one's own.

items.title: Willis Alan Ramsey and the mystery of the one perfect album
items.why: Some songwriters make one record and then spend the rest of their lives being asked about the next one; Willis Alan Ramsey is the patron saint of that club. His 1972 debut is a songwriters' songwriter record, covered all over the map and adored by people like Lyle Lovett. This is a long, careful critical piece from No Depression's criticism fellowship, the sort of album writing that is getting rare.
items.summary: As part of No Depression's criticism fellowship, Erin Osmon writes an in-depth appreciation of Willis Alan Ramsey's self-titled 1972 album on Shelter Records. She looks at why a single record by a little-known Texas songwriter became so widely covered and revered, and at the mystique of a career that never produced a follow-up.

items.title: Caleb Ricks builds a LEGO starship with hardly a right angle in it
items.why: Sci-fi LEGO has been in an arms race of angles for a while, and Caleb Ricks is one of the builders pushing it furthest. The trick worth noticing is the colour: the whole ship was prompted by one of LEGO's newer shades, reddish orange, set against teal and a few odd trans pieces. Look closely at how the angled panels meet without visible gaps.
items.summary: The Brothers Brick features a new spaceship MOC by Caleb Ricks built almost entirely from angled plates and panels. The design was inspired by LEGO's newer reddish orange colour and mixes in teal, white and a splash of trans-light-green.

items.title: floppy3.5: a network share for Sony Mavica floppy disks
items.why: Sony's Mavica cameras saved photos straight onto 3.5-inch floppies, which was briefly the most sensible idea in consumer electronics. This homebrew box puts the floppy drive on the network, and the architecture is the fun part: one microcontroller speaks Greaseweazle to the drive at the flux level, another decodes the data and serves the files. Proper late-90s energy with present-day parts.
items.summary: A hobbyist has built floppy3.5, a small NAS for disks from Sony's floppy-based Mavica digital cameras. An RP2354 reads the drive as a Greaseweazle-compatible device while an ESP32-S3 decodes the raw floppy data and makes the pictures available over the network.

items.title: Carton Clock: a working pendulum clock built from empty drink cartons
items.why: Niklas Roy has form in trash-bin horology, and this time he set himself purist rules after admitting he cheated a little on his earlier clock made of rubbish. Drink cartons, skewers, straws, string, some nuts as weights and a heroic quantity of hot glue get you a full gear train with seconds, minutes and hours. It only runs for about an hour per wind, which seems fair.
items.summary: Artist Niklas Roy built a functioning pendulum clock almost entirely out of empty drink cartons, BBQ skewers, paper straws, string and metal nuts, held together with hot glue. The clockwork drives second, minute and hour displays and runs for a little over an hour when fully wound.

items.title: St. Matthew's Chapel, a little Gothic Revival church in the White Mountains
items.why: New England has no shortage of white churches, but this one in Lisbon, New Hampshire has a reputation as one of the region's most photographed. The pitch is simple: a small Gothic Revival chapel in the White Mountains, foliage in autumn and lupine fields in early summer. Even the build date comes with a small local argument, 1883 or 1893, which is very New England.
items.summary: Atlas Obscura's entry on St. Matthew's Chapel in Lisbon, New Hampshire, a well-kept Gothic Revival church from the late nineteenth century set in the White Mountains. It is popular with photographers for its surroundings in both autumn colour and early-summer lupine season.

items.title: Twenty-five builders raise an occupied Star Wars mountain town at Bricking Bavaria
items.why: Collaborative displays are where LEGO stops being a hobby and turns into civil engineering with a deadline. The Atzen Collab crew lean on Himalayan architecture rather than the usual desert or ice planet, which is why it reads as a lived-in place instead of a set. Worth noticing how much of the Star Wars feel comes from real-world borrowing rather than spaceship greebles.
items.summary: The Atzen Collab, a group of 25 builders, brought a huge diorama to Germany's Bricking Bavaria show: Inwil, a mountain city under Imperial occupation in the Star Wars universe. The Brothers Brick walks through the build, which borrows heavily from Himalayan architecture.

items.title: Comets probably wrecked life's ingredients rather than delivering them
items.why: The comets-seeded-life idea has been a popular-science favourite for about a century, so it is nice to see someone actually do the ballistics. The awkward finding is that impact speeds and angles were mostly wrong for fragile molecules to survive, and Mars comes out slightly better placed than Earth. Asteroids and homegrown chemistry move up the shortlist.
items.summary: Researchers at the University of Cambridge modelled how comets struck the early Earth and concluded that their speeds and impact angles would usually have destroyed the delicate organic molecules they carried. Mars had somewhat better odds, though still slim, which points towards asteroids or chemistry on Earth itself as likelier sources.

items.title: Trying to forecast when a black hole will launch its jets
items.why: Weather forecasting, but for objects that can shut down star formation across a whole neighbourhood. The interesting part is the ambition: moving jet launches from things we catalogue after the fact to things we might predict from a system's state beforehand. A decent tour of where the trigger question stands.
items.summary: Black holes fire powerful jets from their poles that stretch vast distances and can disrupt star formation nearby. New research makes progress on what triggers a launch, with the longer-term aim of predicting when one will happen and learning more about the extreme physics involved.

items.title: Sprite_tm designs his own 486 motherboard and builds a DOS handheld around it
items.why: Plenty of retro handhelds are an emulator in a nice case; this one is a real 486 on a board its maker designed himself, mostly to stop thinking of motherboards as deep magic. He picked the 486 partly because Intel still published proper documentation for ordinary people back then, which says something. The design files are open, even though he doubts anyone will build a second one.
items.summary: Hackaday covers VapourDeck, a homebrew handheld PC built by Sprite_tm around an Intel 486 on a custom motherboard, with a period VGA chip carrying 1MB of video memory. An FPGA handles most glue logic and I/O, an ESP32-S3 does sound, and the design files are published for anyone who wants to try.

items.title: core, a program that shows other programs' memory as pictures and lets you paint on it
items.why: Half esoteric debugger, half paint program, entirely the sort of thing someone builds for the joy of it. Anyone who has stared at a hex dump will recognise the textures it describes: ASCII has its own look, and pointers give themselves away by their mostly-zero top bytes. The suggestion to doodle in the empty space below a process's stack is gloriously irresponsible.
items.summary: The author of core describes a tool that renders a running process's memory on screen and lets you edit it by drawing. The write-up explains how different kinds of data form recognisable patterns, and frames the whole thing as an aimless, meditative way to watch software live.

items.title: Life Beyond Distributed Transactions: Pat Helland's apostasy, via The Morning Paper
items.why: A 2007 classic that aged into conventional wisdom, which is exactly why it rewards a reread. Helland's move is a thought experiment: assume every business entity grows without bound and see which designs survive. Entities, activities and idempotent messaging fall out of it, and a lot of what later got rebranded as microservices and event sourcing is already sitting here.
items.summary: Adrian Colyer's 2014 write-up of Pat Helland's paper on building large applications without distributed transactions, which in practice prove too slow and fragile at scale. Starting from the assumption that the number of customers, orders and other entities grows almost without limit, it names the patterns real systems use instead.

items.title: Clement Wragge's lantern slides on the cosmos and the soul, ca. 1900 to 1922
items.why: Wragge is mostly remembered as the Queensland weatherman who started giving cyclones personal names, reportedly including politicians he disliked. This collection shows his second act as a touring lecturer, with slides ranging from how the universe works to where souls end up. Weather forecasting to metaphysics turns out to be a shorter hop than it sounds.
items.summary: The Public Domain Review gathers lantern slides used by meteorologist Clement Lindley Wragge across some twenty years of public lectures. The images cover astronomy and the workings of the universe alongside his ideas about the fate of the soul.

items.title: A proof of Pythagoras with two tabletops and eight triangles
items.why: No algebra, no fuss: shuffle the same four triangles around a square and look at what is left over. It is the kind of proof that makes you suspicious for about five seconds and then delighted. The picture does all the work, as a good proof picture should.
items.summary: Futility Closet presents a visual proof of the Pythagorean theorem. Four identical right triangles are arranged two ways on equal square tables; one arrangement leaves the square on the hypotenuse uncovered, the other leaves the squares on the two shorter sides, so those areas must match.

items.title: Atlas Obscura's podcast heads east of Calgary, towards the Badlands
items.why: Everyone drives west from Calgary to the mountains; this episode turns the car round. Will Ferguson's opening alone earns it: a hidden valley of wild roses at the edge of the canola fields, holding a small town that has no business being a theatre hub and is one anyway. Good listening for a long bus ride.
items.summary: An Atlas Obscura podcast episode on the unexpected corners of Alberta, with writer Will Ferguson as guide. It starts east of Calgary near the Badlands, in a small valley town that has improbably become a centre for theatre.

items.title: The collared lory, Fiji's scarlet-and-purple parrot that moved into the capital
items.why: A Wikipedia picture of the day, which means a properly good photo and a tidy set of facts. This small lory has taken to life in Suva and will nest in a rotting coconut still hanging on the tree, which is resourceful. Its feathers were once trade goods between Fiji, Samoa and Tonga, so it has an economic history too.
items.summary: Wikipedia's picture of the day for 12 November shows a collared lory perched on an octopus tree. The 20-centimetre parrot lives in Fiji's forests and towns, feeds on fruit, nectar and blossoms, and nests in tree hollows or old coconuts.

items.title: Three photos of a Vogelkop bowerbird in the Arfak Mountains
items.why: Three photos, no essay, which is exactly the right ratio for a bird that lets its architecture do the talking. The Vogelkop is the plain brown bowerbird that compensates by building a hut and curating a front garden of carefully sorted objects. A short hop across the Wallace Line from Penang, as these things go.
items.summary: A 10,000 Birds photo post with three shots of the Vogelkop bowerbird, taken in the Arfak Mountains of West Papua. The species is famous less for its looks than for the elaborate, decorated hut-like bowers the males build to impress females.

items.title: Nine theatrical bird etchings by Jacques de Fornazeris, 1594
items.why: Late sixteenth-century bird art, back when accuracy was optional and attitude was not. These birds pose like actors waiting for their cue, which makes a nice counterpoint to the field-guide realism a birder is used to. Worth a slow scroll with a cup of something.
items.summary: The Public Domain Review gathers a set of nine bird etchings made by Jacques de Fornazeris in 1594. The birds are drawn in a stagey, somewhat stylised manner rather than as naturalist studies.

items.title: Protomaps and PMTiles make self-hosted map tiles cheap and simple
items.why: A satisfying bit of plumbing: the entire world map packed into a single file and served with nothing cleverer than HTTP range requests. No tile server, no per-load API bill, just a bucket and a CDN. Exactly the kind of small, sharp idea that lets hobby map projects survive going viral.
items.summary: A write-up on using the Protomaps ecosystem and its PMTiles format to host your own map tiles. Because the format is one file read through byte-range requests, it can sit on ordinary storage or a CDN, and a command-line tool can cut out just a region or a set of zoom levels.

items.title: A dead star spinning every eight minutes sends radio pulses from 5,000 light-years away
items.why: Eight minutes is a lazy rotation for a stellar corpse and a frantic one for anything else, which is what makes these slow radio pulsers such a puzzle. This one has the decency to come with a Sun-like companion and visible magnetic storms, which gives astronomers something to actually measure.
items.summary: Astronomers have found a binary more than 5,000 light-years away in which a dead star rotates every eight minutes and emits radio pulses while orbiting a Sun-like star. Observations also caught large magnetic storms on the companion, which may help explain this growing class of slow, puzzling radio sources.

items.title: Nuking an incoming asteroid works better if you pick the right side
items.why: Every disaster film assumes the bomb just works; this study asks where to point it. The answer is that a potato-shaped rock reacts very differently depending on which face takes the X-rays, which is a reassuringly nerdy detail to settle well before anyone needs it.
items.summary: New modelling of nuclear asteroid deflection finds that an asteroid's irregular shape strongly shapes how it responds to an X-ray burst. Depending on the angle of the blast, the push delivered varied by nearly a factor of five.

items.title: Please implement a quorum database: the case against reaching for Raft by default
items.why: Part two of a replication rant series, given as a talk at HPTS, arguing that leaderless quorum replication deserves another look in a world where Raft eats everything. The survey slide of who still runs quorums in production is half the fun, Voldemort's ghost included. Opinionated in the good, show-your-working way.
items.summary: A talk write-up making the case for quorum-based data replication as a practical design rather than an academic curiosity. It surveys which databases have used majority quorums, notes several that moved away from them, and walks through why the approach is worth building again.

items.title: Letting uncertainty flow through a dataflow DAG, via The Morning Paper
items.why: A SoCC paper that treats data as distributions with error bars rather than crisp numbers, and makes MapReduce carry those bars through every stage. The GPS example of computed walking speeds above thirty miles an hour is the whole motivation in one line. Old post, still a tidy systems idea.
items.summary: Adrian Colyer's 2018 review of a SoCC paper on propagating uncertainty through data processing pipelines. The authors built UP-MapReduce, adapted ten applications to process uncertain inputs, and report accurate uncertainty estimates at mostly low performance cost.

items.title: PancakeSlicer brings non-planar top surfaces to an ordinary 3D printer
items.why: Non-planar printing has been the jetpack of the 3D printing world: always demoed, rarely shipped. This slicer aims at the modest, achievable bit, smoothing just the top layers on a stock 3-axis printer, and gets there by ray-casting down through the part. Removing the cooling shroud for clearance is a very hacker kind of trade.
items.summary: Hackaday covers PancakeSlicer, a slicer that lays down curved, non-planar top layers on a standard 3-axis printer to avoid the stair-step look. It finds the top surfaces by tracing rays through the model and varies layer thickness continuously, with print-head clearance as the main limit.

items.title: An animated short made entirely in a spreadsheet
items.why: Somebody had to take the phrase cell animation at its word. Maria Tomazou did, and is refreshingly candid that there was no good reason and it took forever. A small tribute to making pointless things for their own sake, which is rather the spirit of this whole feed.
items.summary: Animation director Maria Tomazou made a short film entirely inside Microsoft Excel. She describes it as a long, slightly painful labour with no purpose beyond the making, and is glad she did it anyway.

items.title: The pensioner who out-orbited the astronauts
items.why: A gem of a 1967 letter to a London newspaper in which an old gentleman points out that he has circled the Sun eighty times without a single press conference. Dry British wit aimed squarely at the space race, and still funny.
items.summary: Futility Closet reprints a short 1967 letter to the editor in which a reader born in 1887 mocks the publicity around orbiting astronauts by noting his own eighty trips around the Sun. Everyone does it, he observes, with no ill effects.

items.title: SpaceX catches a Starship upper stage back from orbit for the first time
items.why: A day after the booster catch was waved off, the ship itself came home to the chopsticks, which is the trickier half of the reuse story. Note the flight length too: nearly a full day in orbit before the return, a long way from the suborbital hops of a couple of years ago.
items.summary: SpaceX flew Starship on a record orbital test of about twenty-two and a half hours, then brought the second stage back and caught it in the launch tower's arms. It is the first time the upper stage has been recovered this way after an orbital flight.

items.title: Finding a lunar orbiter's position from its own eclipse shadows
items.why: Flight software people will like this one: no new hardware, just squeezing navigation out of telemetry the spacecraft already produces. With the Deep Space Network oversubscribed, any trick that buys a mission independence from ground tracking is worth a look, and this one is charmingly low-tech.
items.summary: A preprint from researchers at Advanced Space and Texas A&M proposes estimating a spacecraft's orbit around the Moon from the moments its solar arrays drop into and out of eclipse, read off the power telemetry. The idea is to ease the load on NASA's crowded deep-space tracking network at essentially no cost.

items.title: Time protection: making the OS own timing side channels, via The Morning Paper
items.why: This is the EuroSys 2019 best paper that argues timing isolation deserves the same first-class status as memory isolation, rather than a pile of per-attack patches. Worth noticing how much of it comes down to partitioning and flushing hardware state on domain switches, and how candid it is about what current hardware simply won't let software fix.
items.summary: Adrian Colyer walks through Ge and colleagues' proposal of time protection, an OS abstraction meant to close microarchitectural timing channels the way memory protection closes direct access. The work builds on seL4 and covers cache colouring, flushing on switches, and the limits of what can be done in software on today's processors.

items.title: Zwin Nature Park, Belgium's coastal bird reserve and research station
items.why: An interview-style profile of a place that has been ringing, counting and sheltering migrants on the North Sea coast since the 1950s. A good reminder that some of the most useful bird science happens at modest field stations, one net round at a time.
items.summary: The Zwin Nature Park sits in a reserve at the northern tip of the Belgian coast, near the Dutch border, and doubles as an education centre and research station. Its staff describe their monitoring, ringing and conservation work across roughly 560 hectares of salt marsh and dunes.

items.title: An MP3 player built entirely from Factorio's in-game speakers
items.why: Unhappy with the game's simple built-in synth, one player decided the correct response was signal processing in conveyor-belt logic. It is pointless in the best possible way, and the approach rhymes with Fourier analysis done by an assembly line.
items.summary: A Factorio player built a blueprint that plays back recorded music using nothing but the game's programmable speaker entities and circuit network. Since the speakers only offer a handful of instrument voices, the build approximates arbitrary sound by combining many of them, much like decomposing audio into frequencies.

items.title: Seven months building a cycle-accurate-ish NES emulator in Odin
items.why: A refreshingly honest write-up from someone who took the advice that a NES emulator is a weekend job and found out otherwise. The interesting part is the long tail: getting something that boots is quick, getting the last few percent of accuracy is where the months go.
items.summary: A hobbyist describes writing a NES emulator in the Odin language in spare time over about seven months, then pausing it. The post covers what went smoothly, the pain of chasing full accuracy near the end, and why the weekend-project claim misses the hard part.

items.title: Strolling 1920s Berlin with Franz Hessel, the flâneur who looked away
items.why: Hessel's walking book of Berlin earned Walter Benjamin's admiration, and this essay takes it seriously while asking what a stroller in late Weimar Berlin chose not to notice. A nice slow read for anyone who likes cities read on foot.
items.summary: A Public Domain Review essay by Paul Sullivan follows Franz Hessel through the streets of 1920s Berlin as recorded in his book of city walks. It weighs the charm and the blind spots of his gentle, apolitical way of seeing a city on the brink.

items.title: James Felice goes big and strange on his second solo album, Homeworld Blue
items.why: The Felice Brothers' accordionist made a quiet solo debut last year; this one, by the reviewer's account, swings the other way, with grand arrangements dreamed up in his attic. Worth a listen if you like your Americana with a bit of cosmic weather in it.
items.summary: No Depression reviews James Felice's new album, made over about four years and recorded in Omaha with Nathaniel Walcott producing. The review describes it as sweeping and surreal, a big contrast with the hushed songs of his 2025 debut.

items.title: Why some Apollo crews took a grenade launcher to the Moon
items.why: It sounds like a pub-quiz trap, but the answer is pure geophysics: small explosive charges lobbed across the surface make seismic waves you can read. A good example of Apollo-era engineers solving a science problem with whatever worked, and a lively thread of people who know the hardware.
items.summary: A space Q and A thread explains the mortar package carried on some Apollo landings as part of an active seismic experiment. Grenades fired to different distances set off small shocks picked up by geophones, letting scientists probe the structure of the ground beneath the landing site.

items.title: MEUTE, an eleven-piece marching band that plays techno
items.why: Brass, drums and mallets doing what synthesisers usually do, with enough discipline to keep a club groove going acoustically. A cheerful few minutes, and a nice argument that a genre is a set of ideas rather than a set of machines.
items.summary: MEUTE is a German group that performs techno and house tracks on acoustic instruments in marching-band style: tubas, trombones, saxophones, percussion and more. The new single comes from their latest album, Kosmos.

items.title: Fossil teeth hint that coastal dinosaurs were eating from the sea
items.why: Every dinosaur diet story is ultimately a story about teeth, and this one reads the chemistry rather than the wear marks. The fun part is the idea of seaweed-derived nutrients working their way up a Cretaceous food chain, so even a land-bound herbivore could be carrying a little of the ocean in its enamel.
items.summary: Researchers found chemical signatures in fossilised teeth suggesting that coastal dinosaurs and their neighbours, more than 100 million years ago, drew part of their nutrition from marine sources such as seaweed. The signal turns up in both plant-eaters and predators, pointing to sea-derived food moving through whole ancient ecosystems.

items.title: Euclid finds 31 distant quasars, two of them record-breakers
items.why: Euclid was built to map dark matter, so turning up a haul of early-universe quasars is a rather good side hustle. Worth noticing is the age: these black holes were already blazing when the cosmos was a few hundred million years old, which keeps sharpening the question of how anything got that big that fast.
items.summary: ESA's Euclid telescope has identified 31 ancient quasars, including two exceptionally luminous ones seen when the universe was about 670 million years old. Each is powered by a supermassive black hole feeding at a furious rate while the first galaxies were still assembling.

items.title: Live migration for bhyve guests on FreeBSD, a first working cut
items.why: Live migration is one of those features that sounds like a checkbox until you have to write the dirty-page tracking yourself. This one does it the honest way: pre-copy over TCP, dirty bits tracked in the vmm module, and a short stop-and-copy at the end. A tidy look at the plumbing for anyone who has stared at a hypervisor's memory map.
items.summary: A developer presents a working prototype of live migration for bhyve virtual machines on FreeBSD 15.1, moving a running amd64 guest between hosts with only a brief pause at the end. It builds on bhyve's experimental snapshot code and adds dirty-page tracking in the kernel's vmm module plus a migration protocol in the userland tools.

items.title: Swapping DRAM for NVM under MyRocks at Facebook, via The Morning Paper
items.why: A EuroSys paper with an unusually practical bent: not 'what if NVM' but 'here is what happened when we put it under a production database.' The interesting bits are the access-pattern tricks needed to hide NVM's latency and wear limits, which read a lot like the old buffer-cache tuning wars with new hardware.
items.summary: Adrian Colyer's write-up of a 2018 study on using non-volatile memory devices to shrink the DRAM footprint of MyRocks, Facebook's RocksDB-based MySQL storage engine. It covers how the team placed caches on NVM, coped with its latency and endurance limits, and what it saved in cost and power.

items.title: DIVINER turns a pocket Cardputer into an occult synthesizer
items.why: The M5 Cardputer is a tiny keyboard-and-screen ESP32 board begging for weird firmware, and DIVINER answers with something between a synth, a sequencer and a fortune-telling toy. It is exactly the kind of gleeful, slightly pointless hobby project that made the early web fun.
items.summary: DIVINER is a firmware for the M5 Cardputer, an ESP32-S3 handheld with a miniature screen, keyboard and audio output. It packs a standalone synthesizer and sequencer alongside a grab-bag of mystical-themed features, all running on a device that fits in a palm.

items.title: Chasing chats around Spitzkoppe, Namibia's granite island
items.why: A trip report with a sense of humour about its own setting, plus a target bird most of us have never heard of. The Herero Chat is a near-endemic of the Namibian escarpment, and a granite inselberg glowing orange at dawn is about as good a backdrop for a little brown job as one could ask for.
items.summary: A birder visits Spitzkoppe, a cluster of granite peaks rising some 700 metres above the Namibian plain, in search of the region's chats, including the Herero Chat. The post mixes the landscape, the birds found and the gentle absurdity of comparing the place to the Matterhorn.

items.title: Punch Brothers play the University at Buffalo's Center for the Arts on November 15
items.why: Favourite-band rule applies, and the tour keeps rolling west of Ithaca. Not much detail in the listing itself, but a Punch Brothers night in a university hall is reliably a lesson in how five acoustic instruments can sound like a chamber orchestra with a sense of humour.
items.summary: A local listing notes that Punch Brothers are performing at the Center for the Arts at the University at Buffalo on November 15, another stop on their current tour. The piece is a brief event notice rather than a review.

items.title: The Mother of the Sea statue in Nuuk, Greenland
items.why: Most harbour statues commemorate someone; this one is a story told in bronze, and it doubles as a quiet nag about how we treat the ocean. Even better, it sits in the water and goes under with the tide, so whether you see her depends on when you show up.
items.summary: On the Nuuk shoreline stands a sculpture of Sassuma Arnaa, the Mother of the Sea from Kalaallit tradition, who withholds the sea animals when people stop respecting the balance with the ocean. The statue is placed so that the rising tide covers it, tying the old tale to the shore it watches.

items.title: The Arecibo message, and the prime trick behind its layout
items.why: The Arecibo message is the classic thought experiment in alien-friendly encoding: make the length a semiprime and hope the reader takes the hint. It still makes a good humility check for anyone who has ever designed a file format and assumed the reader would just know.
items.summary: In 1974 the Arecibo telescope beamed a 1,679-bit message toward the globular cluster M13; since 1,679 is the product of two primes, the bits can be laid out as a 23-by-73 picture showing numbers, DNA chemistry, a human figure and the telescope itself. Futility Closet walks through what the message encodes and how its layout is meant to be discovered.

items.title: How the Intel 8087 computed tangents: CORDIC plus a polynomial
items.why: Ken Shirriff's tour through the 8087 keeps finding little works of art in the silicon, and this one is the trig unit. The neat trick is that Intel didn't pick between CORDIC and polynomial approximation; it used both, trading a few cycles for accuracy that held up in an era when a coprocessor was a luxury.
items.summary: A die-level reverse-engineering of the tangent instruction in Intel's 1980 8087 floating-point coprocessor. Shirriff traces how the chip combined a CORDIC-style rotation stage with a polynomial approximation, and how the microcode and datapath carry it out.

items.title: Punch Brothers take The Unsung Adventures to Europe, their first tour there in nearly a decade
items.why: After a long North American run, Chris Thile and company are pointing the van across the Atlantic for the first time in close to ten years. Worth noting that the album they are touring is the all-instrumental one, so European audiences get the band at its most chamber-music-with-banjo. If a Penang-to-Europe winter trip ever needed an excuse, here it is.
items.summary: Punch Brothers have announced a European tour in support of The Unsung Adventures of Punch Brothers, their first all-instrumental record. It is the band's first tour of Europe in nearly a decade, with dates booked for early 2027.

items.title: Recovering from metastable failures: find the loop before you restart
items.why: Aleksey Charapko takes a fresh cloud outage, where servers went unresponsive again as soon as traffic returned, and reads it as a textbook metastable failure. The useful bit is the framing: recovery means locating and breaking the sustaining feedback loop, not just removing the trigger. Anyone who has watched a retry storm re-kill a freshly rebooted fleet will nod along.
items.summary: A short essay on recovering from metastable failures, prompted by a recent large outage in which restored servers fell over again once they took load. Charapko recaps how such failures start with a trigger but persist through a self-sustaining loop, and argues that recovery work should focus on identifying where that loop lives.

items.title: A Hazeltine 1420 terminal brought back from the dead
items.why: Before every computer came with a screen, you picked a terminal, and Hazeltine was one of the names on the shortlist. This restoration has everything: tired capacitors, a transistor someone pinched for another unit, scorched rectifiers and irreplaceable character ROMs. Bonus points for documenting the early decisions that came back to bite.
items.summary: The Byte Attic revived a non-working Hazeltine 1420 video terminal, replacing failing capacitors and a missing power transistor and swapping the hot linear regulators for switching ones. Because the character-set chips can no longer be bought, the project also reads them out so replacements can be made before they die.

items.title: KDE: the documentary, thirty years of a free desktop
items.why: KDE turned thirty in October, and the project marked it with a documentary about how a 1996 call for volunteers to build a consistent Unix desktop became one of free software's longest-running communities. This is exactly the late-90s optimism the feed exists for. It is hosted on PeerTube, which is a very KDE way to publish a film.
items.summary: A feature-length documentary on the history of the KDE project, released for its thirtieth anniversary. It traces the desktop from its origins in the mid-1990s through the people and communities that have kept it going, and drew a big crowd on Hacker News.

items.title: Eight birds named after other birds
items.why: Zebra Finch is easy: nobody confuses it with a zebra. It gets murkier when the borrowed name belongs to another bird, and you end up with cuckooshrikes that are neither cuckoos nor shrikes. A light, well-made list with the original namesakes laid side by side, and a fine excuse to argue about common names on your next solo walk.
items.summary: 10,000 Birds rounds up eight species whose common names come from resembling a different bird, such as the cuckooshrikes. A table pairs each one with the bird it was named after, untangling which is the real thing and which got the name for its looks.

items.title: Form or function: how Gnarlicbread builds LEGO mechs
items.why: Every mech builder eventually has to choose between a model that poses and a model that looks good on the shelf. BrickNerd sits down with Gnarlicbread to hear how they handle that trade-off. Mechs are where LEGO joint technique gets its hardest workout, so there is plenty to steal here.
items.summary: A BrickNerd interview and builder showcase featuring Gnarlicbread, known for LEGO mechs. The piece looks at how the builder balances appearance against articulation and playability in their designs.

items.title: A Pakistani astronaut will be the first foreigner aboard China's Tiangong
items.why: Tiangong has been a strictly domestic affair since its first module went up, so the first international visitor is a real milestone. The seat goes to a Pakistani astronaut flying with the Shenzhou 24 crew, about two weeks out. Worth watching as the station quietly becomes a second option for countries outside the ISS club.
items.summary: The China Manned Space Agency plans to fly an astronaut from Pakistan to the Tiangong space station on the Shenzhou 24 mission, due in about two weeks. It will be the first time anyone from outside China has visited the station.

items.title: Looking for Einstein in the Moon's tides
items.why: Tides are the most Newtonian thing imaginable, which is precisely why a relativistic fingerprint in them would be interesting. A Berlin theorist has worked out how to search high-precision measurements of the lunar tides for the subtle traces general relativity should leave. A nice reminder that a lot of physics hides in the decimal places.
items.summary: A researcher at Freie Universitat Berlin has built a theoretical framework for detecting possible relativistic effects in the Moon's tides. The idea is to sift existing high-precision measurements for small signatures that classical Newtonian tidal theory would not predict.

items.title: Tin Lizzy Ice Cream Man, an out-of-work fiberglass giant in Indiana
items.why: Roadside fiberglass giants are a fine American art form, and this one has the added indignity of an empty cone. The shop is long closed, the paint is peeling, and he still stands at the crossroads near Montpelier. Parks and Recreation fans may recognise him from the first season's opening credits.
items.summary: A large fiberglass mascot still stands outside the closed Tin Lizzy Ice Cream Shop at a rural crossroads west of Montpelier, Indiana. Faded and missing the ice cream from his cone, he once appeared in the opening titles of Parks and Recreation's first season.

items.title: Solving the Feynman restaurant problem
items.why: Feynman's question is the classic explore-versus-exploit dilemma wearing a napkin: how many dishes do you try before settling on your favourite? The worked answer has a satisfying punchline, once you commit, order that dish every remaining visit. Applicable to kopitiams, record shops and scheduler design alike.
items.summary: Kottke points to a solution of the Feynman restaurant problem, which asks how many different dishes you should sample at a restaurant to maximise your enjoyment over a fixed number of visits. The answer is to explore for a while, then stick with the best dish found for the rest of your visits.

items.title: Eleanor McEvoy brings A Woman's Heart to Irvine's Harbour Arts Centre
items.why: A favourite-artist sighting, so it goes straight in. McEvoy wrote the title song of the best-selling Irish album of its era, and she has spent the decades since proving she is more than that one song while still singing it beautifully. A small Scottish arts centre on the Ayrshire coast is about the right size of room for her.
items.summary: The Irish singer-songwriter Eleanor McEvoy has a date at the Harbour Arts Centre in Irvine, on the Ayrshire coast. Her signature song, A Woman's Heart, is billed as part of the evening.

items.title: John Manley, the Marblehead captain who kept the siege of Boston supplied
items.why: Everyone remembers Dorchester Heights; fewer remember where the powder came from. Manley's story is the sea-going footnote to the siege of Boston, back when the Continental navy was a handful of armed schooners and a lot of nerve. Good reading for anyone who has walked the Marblehead waterfront and wondered.
items.summary: In 1775 Washington's army had the British bottled up in Boston but was desperately short of arms and gunpowder. This piece tells how John Manley, commanding one of the first armed vessels sailing for the patriots, captured British supply ships and kept the siege going, and why he is so little remembered.

items.title: A ZIP archive that boots itself
items.why: The kernel will happily unpack a CPIO archive into early userspace; this author wondered how far that tolerance can be bent, and ended up with a file that is a valid ZIP and a bootable image at once. Polyglot files are one of computing's great harmless mischiefs, and this one comes with real initramfs plumbing to chew on.
items.summary: Starting from the way Linux unpacks a CPIO archive into initramfs, the author works out how to build a single file that standard ZIP tools can open and that can also be booted. The post walks through the archive formats and the low-level tricks needed to make both readers happy.

items.title: Reverse-engineering Score Perfect to rescue a father's music files
items.why: Data preservation usually fails not with a bang but with a program nobody maintains any more. Here a son takes his father's years of notation files out of an abandoned format by working out the format itself, which is the most loving kind of reverse engineering there is. Worth noticing how small the job becomes once one person bothers.
items.summary: Score Perfect, a music notation program, stopped being developed in 2012, leaving a lifetime of files stuck in its own format. Maarten Tromp reverse engineered that format so his father's scores could be converted and carried over to modern notation software.

items.title: Solving the fox game: do the foxes or the sheep win with perfect play?
items.why: An old Norse board game in which twenty sheep try to slip past two foxes, an open question about who wins with perfect play, and a programmer who could not leave it alone. The family folklore said the foxes had it easy. Retrograde analysis has opinions about family folklore.
items.summary: After another writer's AI experiments left the question open, the author set out to solve halatafl, the asymmetric fox-and-sheep game, outright. The post covers how the game's state space was searched and what the answer turns out to be.

items.title: Dark energy may have flipped sign about 9.5 billion years ago
items.why: The idea that dark energy is a fixed constant has been under strain since the DESI results, and theorists are now exploring what a changing one would look like. This one comes from a neglected corner of a modified-gravity theory, so file it under interesting possibility rather than settled fact. Still, a sign flip is a bold claim to have on the table.
items.summary: Researchers working with an overlooked branch of an alternative theory of gravity found that dark energy could have switched from negative to positive roughly 9.5 billion years ago. If borne out, it would change the story of how the universe's expansion has evolved.

items.title: RAMP transactions: atomic visibility without the coordination, via The Morning Paper
items.why: Bailis and friends asked how much isolation you can keep across partitions without paying for locks or a central coordinator, and RAMP was the elegant answer: readers can detect and repair a fractured view on their own. Colyer's write-up is a good refresher on why this was the clever bit behind the coordination-avoidance results.
items.summary: A summary of the 2014 paper on Read Atomic Multi-Partition transactions, which guarantee that either all or none of a transaction's writes are visible across a partitioned database. It explains the problem of fractured reads and how RAMP uses metadata to avoid them without blocking.

items.title: In praise of the American Coot
items.why: The coot is the bird everyone scrolls past on the lake on the way to something rarer, which is exactly why it deserves an advocate. Those lobed toes and that improbable chick are worth a second look. Penang has its own rails and moorhens, so consider this one a cousin from away.
items.summary: A republished archive piece arguing that the American Coot, the most abundant and widespread rail in North America, gets far less respect than it deserves. It makes the case for the bird's oddities and charms.

items.title: Pensão Amor, a former sailors' brothel in Lisbon turned bar
items.why: Cais do Sodré used to be where sailors, fado singers, writers and the odd spy all ended up, and this building keeps that cast of characters in its decor. Velvet and red light rather than azulejos for once. A good evening stop after a day of trams and hills.
items.summary: On Lisbon's Pink Street in the old port district, a building that once served as a brothel has been reborn as a theatrical bar, with plush rooms and decor that nods to the sailors and night owls who once filled the quarter.

items.title: Stupendously large black holes ruled out as dark matter
items.why: Somewhere a physicist had to write 'SLAB' in a serious paper and keep a straight face, and for that alone this deserves a look. The interesting part is the method of elimination: each dark matter candidate struck off narrows the room left for the rest. Not a discovery so much as a very tidy no.
items.summary: Primordial black holes have long been floated as a possible answer to dark matter, and SLABs are an especially heavy variety of them. New research finds that these stupendously large black holes cannot make up the missing mass either, trimming another option from the list.

items.title: Chandra finds the hidden companion behind a giant star's repeated outbursts
items.why: A giant star in another galaxy has been throwing fits for at least fifteen years, and the culprit turns out to be a roommate nobody could see. X-rays did what visible light couldn't. A nice case of the boring explanation, a binary, being far more fun than the exotic one.
items.summary: Astronomers using NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory found a previously unseen black hole or neutron star orbiting a massive, unstable star. The companion appears to be what keeps triggering the star's recurring eruptions.

items.title: Audubon's new report on bird population trends across Latin America and the Caribbean
items.why: Most of the long-running bird trend data comes from north of the Rio Grande, so a regional picture for Latin America and the Caribbean fills a real gap. Note how much of it rests on volunteers with binoculars and checklists, which is exactly the kind of community science a solo birder in Penang feeds into too.
items.summary: Audubon has published a report on how bird populations are changing across Latin America and the Caribbean. It draws heavily on community science data and argues that volunteer observations are becoming a powerful tool for tracking birds in the region.

items.title: Punch Brothers headline a weekend at Ithaca's State Theatre
items.why: More Punch Brothers dates keep surfacing ahead of the PB&J run with Jeff Tweedy, and this one puts them on a historic stage in a college town that knows its string bands. The bill shares the weekend with drag comedy, which is a very Ithaca sort of programme.
items.summary: Punch Brothers are among the headliners of a weekend run at the State Theatre in Ithaca, New York. Jinkx Monsoon and BenDeLaCreme round out the theatre's weekend line-up.

items.title: CoDel and adaptive LIFO: borrowing bufferbloat fixes for server queues, via The Morning Paper
items.why: Anyone who followed the bufferbloat saga in the networking stack will recognise CoDel; the fun here is watching it escape the qdisc layer and get applied to RPC request queues. Adrian Colyer pairs the Nichols and Jacobson paper with Ben Maurer's account of Facebook's reliability work, and the adaptive LIFO trick is the bit worth stealing.
items.summary: An archive write-up from The Morning Paper on two pieces: the Controlled Delay queue management algorithm, and an ACM Queue article on keeping a huge service reliable. It focuses on the strategies for resource exhaustion, namely CoDel, adaptive last-in-first-out queuing and concurrency control.

items.title: Borland C++ 2.0 rebuilt from its binaries, byte for byte
items.why: Borland never released the source, so someone worked backwards from the shipped toolchain until the reconstructed compiler produced identical output. That 'byte-perfect' claim is the whole game: it means the result is checkable, not merely plausible. Handy for anyone poking at DOS-era software, and a lovely bit of digital palaeontology besides.
items.summary: The 1991 Borland C++ 2.0 toolchain, successor to Turbo C++, has been reconstructed as source code that is claimed to compile into binaries identical to the originals. The process, which used a tool built on an AI coding assistant, is documented separately.

items.title: Freeing a Coway air purifier from its cloud
items.why: A classic itch-scratch: the goal was only to make the fan crank up when the 'Good Night' button turns the lights off, and the route there ran through someone else's cloud service. The writeup is a tidy tour of poking at a consumer gadget until it talks to you locally. The late-90s spirit, applied to a box fan with a filter.
items.summary: A Bay Area homeowner who relies on a Coway air purifier for wildfire smoke and white noise wanted it integrated with his home automation. He reverse engineered the device so it could be controlled locally rather than through the manufacturer's cloud.

items.title: The world's oldest leather shoe, on show in Yerevan
items.why: A single piece of cowhide, laces still in it, and roughly a modern size 7. It survived five and a half thousand years because the cave was sealed under layers of sheep dung, which is the least glamorous preservation method imaginable and apparently one of the best.
items.summary: A leather shoe found in 2008 in the Areni-1 cave in Armenia has been radiocarbon dated to around 3600 to 3500 BC. Stuffed with grass and nearly intact thanks to the cool, dry cave, it is now displayed in the Armenian capital.

items.title: Revisiting Ladyhawke, the medieval romance with a synth score
items.why: Ladyhawke is the eighties fantasy film people either adore or remember mostly for its Alan Parsons Project soundtrack. Reactor's 80s Fantasy Film Club column gives it a fair hearing, cursed lovers, a young Matthew Broderick and all. Good company for a quiet evening.
items.summary: A column looking back at the 1985 film in which a knight and his love are cursed by a bishop to live as a wolf and a hawk, never human at the same time. It considers what the film does well and how its odd mix of medieval setting and synthesiser music has aged.

items.title: Sicily and the family tree of citrus
items.why: Food history with a map in its heart: the Conca d'Oro outside Palermo, irrigated by Arab engineers into something they thought of as paradise, and the citron at the root of the whole citrus family. Kottke points to an illustrated eight-part series that is a pleasure to wander through.
items.summary: Kottke highlights Erik Gauger's illustrated series on citrus fruit and Sicily. It traces how Arab irrigation turned the plain around Palermo into a famed garden and how the citron ties into the island's cultural and culinary history.

items.title: Starship flies, but SpaceX waves off the first booster catch
items.why: The plan was to bring both stages home for the first time, which is the whole reason the thing is meant to be cheap. Instead the launch-pad catch of the booster was called off on safety grounds, a reminder that 'we chose not to' is a perfectly respectable flight-software outcome. Watch for what the abort logic decided and when.
items.summary: SpaceX launched another Starship flight intended to recover both the booster and the upper stage. The booster's catch at the launch tower was cancelled over safety concerns, so the flight went ahead without that milestone.

items.title: LOFAR makes the deepest low-frequency radio map of the sky yet
items.why: LOFAR is the delightfully unglamorous telescope made of thousands of small antennas scattered across the Dutch countryside and beyond, stitched together in software. A Leiden-led team has squeezed the sharpest, most sensitive low-frequency image yet out of it, which mostly means a great many faint galaxies nobody had heard before. A nice case of the correlator being the real instrument.
items.summary: Astronomers led by Leiden University used the Low Frequency Array to produce the most sensitive and highest-resolution image of the sky ever made at low radio frequencies. The survey reveals huge numbers of faint radio sources, many of them distant galaxies.

items.title: A map of where the fossil record is still blank
items.why: Not a new beast this time but a map of where the new beasts are likely hiding. An analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils finds that some of the richest unexplored ground lies in comparatively young rocks, not the deep past everyone romanticises. Useful for anyone deciding where to point a rock hammer next.
items.summary: Researchers analysed half a billion years of marine fossil records to find gaps in what has been sampled. They conclude that many undiscovered species probably sit in relatively recent geological periods, and have mapped under-explored fossil-bearing regions to guide future digs.

items.title: Species Spotlight: the Black Woodpecker and its taste in beech
items.why: Europe's biggest woodpecker is a picky property developer: in French forests it prefers to dig its nest holes in beech-dominated stands with few skinny trees cluttering the view. 10,000 Birds runs it as a real-estate joke, but the habitat science underneath is real, and the photo alone earns the click.
items.summary: A short species profile of the Black Woodpecker, the crow-sized woodpecker of Eurasian forests. It looks at where the bird chooses to excavate, noting studies showing a preference for beech-rich sites with fewer small-diameter trees.

items.title: What Europe might want to be in 2050
items.why: Timothy Taylor does his usual service of reading the stack so you don't have to: CEPR has gathered dozens of papers on what the EU should aim to look like by mid-century. Thinking in decades instead of quarters is refreshingly calm, and Taylor picks out the threads worth following without selling a thesis.
items.summary: The Conversable Economist introduces a CEPR project, led by Olivier Blanchard, Pascal Lamy, Enrico Letta and Beatrice Weder di Mauro, collecting essays on Europe's long-term economic, environmental and foreign-policy future. Taylor highlights several of the contributions and the questions they raise.

items.title: St. Patrick's Church, Cape Breton's oldest surviving Catholic church
items.why: A stone church in Sydney, Nova Scotia whose origin story involves a grieving couple, a garrison captain and the awkward fact that Catholics then couldn't easily own land or bury their dead. The workaround that followed is the interesting bit; the reported ghosts are optional extras for the gift shop crowd.
items.summary: St. Patrick's in Sydney's historic North End is the oldest surviving Catholic church on Cape Breton Island. Its history begins in the 1780s with the burial of a garrison captain's infant son at a time when restrictions on Catholics left the town without a Catholic cemetery.

items.title: A literary map of the United States, real towns and imaginary ones
items.why: A map that plots the settings of hundreds of American books, with Sleepy Hollow and East Egg sitting on the same roads as real places. Frank Jacobs's look at the invented towns on it gets into imaginative geography, which is a fancy name for why fictional places feel like you could drive there.
items.summary: Big Think and Pop Charts made a map of the United States marked with the settings of hundreds of novels and stories. A companion piece examines the fictional places on it, from Lake Wobegon to Fitzgerald's Eggs, and what they reveal about American literature.

items.title: tranZPUter: modern drop-in replacements for vintage CPUs
